title: Ἄνθρωποι καὶ Ζεύς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 57. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέγουσι πρῶτον τὰ ζῷα πλασθῆναι καὶ χαρισθῆναι αὐτοῖς παρὰ θεοῦ, τῷ μὲν ἀλκήν, τῷ δὲ τάχος, τῷ δὲ πτερά, τὸν δὲ ἄνθρωπον γυμνὸν ἑστῶτα εἰπεῖν· « Ἐμὲ μόνον κατέλιπες ἔρημον χάριτος· » τὸν δὲ Δία εἰπεῖν· « Ἀνεπαίσθητος εἶ τῆς δωρεᾶς, καίτοι τοῦ μεγίστου τετυχηκώς· λόγον γὰρ ἔχεις λαβών, ὃς παρὰ θεοῖς δύναται καὶ παρὰ ἀνθρώποις, τῶν δυνατῶν δυνατώτερος καὶ τῶν ταχίστων ταχύτερος. »
sentences.tr: Legousi prōton ta zōia plasthēnai kai charisthēnai autois para theou, tōi men alkēn, tōi de tachos, tōi de ptera, ton de anthrōpon gymnon hestōta eipein· « Eme monon katelipes erēmon charitos· » ton de Dia eipein· « Anepaisthētos ei tēs dōreas, kaitoi tou megistou tetychēkōs· logon gar echeis labōn, hos para theois dynatai kai para anthrōpois, tōn dynatōn dynatōteros kai tōn tachistōn tachyteros. »
sentences.l: They say that first the animals were formed and that gifts were granted to them by a god — to one strength, to another speed, to another wings — but that man, standing naked, said: « Me alone you have left destitute of a gift; » and that Zeus said: « You are insensible of the gift, although you have obtained the greatest one; for you have reason, having received it, which has power among gods and among men, more powerful than the powerful and swifter than the swiftest. »
sentences.i: They say that the animals were formed first and that a god granted gifts to them — to one strength, to another speed, to another wings — but that man, standing there naked, said: « Me alone you have left with no gift at all, » and that Zeus answered: « You have no feeling for the gift, though you have obtained the greatest of all: you have been given reason, which is powerful among gods and among men, mightier than the mighty and swifter than the swiftest. »
sentences.n: Λέγουσι governs a whole chain of accusative-and-infinitive — πλασθῆναι, χαρισθῆναι, εἰπεῖν, εἰπεῖν — so everything that follows stands in reported speech, 'they say that…'. τῷ μὲν … τῷ δὲ … τῷ δέ is the distributive 'to one … to another … to another'. λόγος means at once speech and reason, and the fable lives off the double sense. καίτοι τοῦ μεγίστου τετυχηκώς, 'although having obtained the greatest'; τυγχάνω takes its object in the genitive.

sentences.t: Καὶ τότε ἐπιγνοὺς τὸ δῶρον ὁ ἄνθρωπος προσκυνήσας καὶ εὐχαριστήσας ᾤχετο.
sentences.tr: Kai tote epignous to dōron ho anthrōpos proskynēsas kai eucharistēsas ōicheto.
sentences.l: And then the man, having-recognized the gift, having-made-obeisance and having-given-thanks, went away.
sentences.i: And then the man, recognizing the gift, bowed down, gave thanks, and went his way.
sentences.n: Three aorist participles hung on a single main verb (ἐπιγνούς, προσκυνήσας, εὐχαριστήσας … ᾤχετο) — the ordinary engine of a fable's narrative, each step complete before the next begins. προσκυνέω is the bodily gesture of prostration before a god or a king, not merely inward reverence.

sentences.t: Ὅτι, ἐκ θεοῦ λόγῳ τιμηθέντων πάντων, ἀνεπαισθήτως ἔχουσί τινες τῆς τοιαύτης τιμῆς καὶ μᾶλλον ζηλοῦσι τὰ ἀναίσθητα καὶ ἄλογα ζῷα.
sentences.tr: Hoti, ek theou logōi timēthentōn pantōn, anepaisthētōs echousi tines tēs toiautēs timēs kai mallon zēlousi ta anaisthēta kai aloga zōia.
sentences.l: That, all having been honoured by a god with reason, some are without perception of such honour and rather envy the senseless and reasonless animals.
sentences.i: The story shows that, though god honoured all men with reason, some have no feeling for such honour and would sooner envy the beasts, which have neither sense nor speech.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the 'the story shows' is unexpressed in the Greek, which opens simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. τιμηθέντων πάντων is a genitive absolute and λόγῳ a dative of means, 'by means of reason'. ἀνεπαισθήτως ἔχειν with the genitive is 'to have no perception of' — ἔχω with an adverb regularly stands for 'to be' in a given state. ἄλογα picks up λόγον from above: the beasts are precisely 'without reason', the one thing man was given.
